forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Darlington's debt fell by £5.1m but reserves are funding growth in capital spending
news_drafts.lead: Darlington Council reduced its external debt by £5.1m to £167.6m in 2025/26, repaying a maturing loan and taking no new borrowing. The reduction was enabled by slippage of £17.6m in the capital programme, with most delay in housing and regeneration schemes. However, the council's underlying need to borrow for long-lived assets remains substantial at £249.9m. The gap of £73.8m between this capital financing requirement and actual debt is being covered by drawing on cash reserves rather than external borrowing. While this strategy currently saves money because borrowing costs exceed investment returns, the council's investment portfolio shrank to £25m after a forced distribution from its Hermes property fund following a merger. Bank rate cuts stalled at 3.75%, with markets expecting rates to remain static through 2026/27, limiting scope for refinancing savings. The council's treasury budget overspent by £0.8m, driven by lower property fund dividends and changes to repayment schedules for the Feethams House project.

findings.paper_title: 260924 RG Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Bank rate fell only 0.25 percentage points to 3.75%; market expects rates static through 2026/27, limiting refinancing savings.
findings.detail: The bank rate fell from 4.0% at the start of 2025/26 to 3.75% by 31 March 2026. Interest rate forecasts initially suggested more gradual reductions, but these proved overly optimistic. The market now expects the bank rate to remain static throughout 2026/27 due to global economic uncertainty, with a risk of increases if inflation rises. This significantly constrains the opportunity to refinance existing debt at lower rates.
findings.matters: Slower rate cuts than anticipated reduce the council's refinancing flexibility and extend the period during which the under-borrowing strategy is necessary. If rates remain elevated or rise, the council's cost of servicing maturing debt will be higher than initially budgeted.
findings.figures: Bank rate fell from 4.0% to 3.75% (25bp reduction); market expects rates static through 2026/27
findings.quote: The bank rate was 4% at the start of the year and cuts have been cautious primarily because inflation concerns remained elevated. The bank rate as at 31st March 2026 was 3.75%. The market now expects the bank rate to remain fairly static throughout 2026/27, due to uncertainty with the global economy and the impact this could have on inflation.

findings.paper_title: 260924 RG Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Council under-borrowed by £73.790m, using cash reserves instead of external borrowing, creating future refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The council's capital financing requirement was £249.881m but external debt was only £176.091m. The £73.790m gap was financed using internal reserves rather than borrowing. While this saves money currently (borrowing costs exceed investment returns), the strategy is dependent on maintaining adequate cash reserves and creates exposure to refinancing shock once reserves are depleted or drawn for operational purposes.
findings.matters: The under-borrowed position reduces immediate borrowing costs but increases refinancing risk. A lender needs to understand the trajectory of reserve depletion and the council's ability to service future borrowing if interest rates remain elevated or if capital demands spike.
findings.quote: The reduced under borrowed position still has the dual effect of reducing costs to the MTFP, because borrowing costs are generally greater than investment returns and it reduces counterparty risk by reducing our exposure to banks and other financial institutions.

findings.paper_title: 260924 RG Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Forced to redeem £8.896m from Hermes property fund following merger; deployed to debt repayment.
findings.detail: The Hermes Federated property fund merged with a larger fund and only pension funds were eligible to transfer. The council received a forced distribution of £8.896m, which was used to repay short-term maturing debt. This left the council's investment portfolio reduced from £35.408m to £25.055m and eliminated a source of longer-term investment returns (from 3.74% gross).
findings.matters: The forced disposal removes a diversified investment asset and flexibility for the council, reduces income-generating capacity, and shows the council is increasingly dependent on cash management and debt repayment rather than investment returns.
findings.figures: £8.896m distribution; investments fell from £35.408m to £25.055m; property fund average return fell from 3.74% gross to 4.12% gross on smaller base
findings.quote: Hermes Federated merged with a larger fund and under the terms of the merger only pension funds were eligible to transfer into the merged fund. The Council therefore received a cash distribution of £8.896m as its share of the fund. This funding has been used to repay debt that was maturing in the short term to save on interest costs whilst options for longer term investments are investigated.

findings.paper_title: 260924 RG Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure underspent by £17.603m (26.7% of plan), with majority in HRA and Towns Fund schemes.
findings.detail: Planned capital spend of £65.944m was not achieved; actual expenditure was £49.479m. The variance was primarily driven by housing revenue account underspend of £10.145m and slippage in Towns Fund initiatives. This reduced the borrowing need by £8.603m but raises questions about programme delivery and whether targets are realistic.
findings.matters: Large-scale capital slippage may indicate delivery challenges, resource constraints, or strategic changes. For a lender, it signals uncertainty about whether the council can execute its capital strategy, and delays the point at which long-term financing will be needed.
findings.figures: £49.479m actual vs £65.944m revised plan; £17.603m variance; HRA variance £10.145m
findings.quote: Actual expenditure was £17.603m less than planned, mostly down to slippage in the HRA, and Towns Fund initiatives.

findings.paper_title: 260924 RG Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Financing costs overspent by £0.834m, driven by lower property fund dividends and MRP reprofiling.
findings.detail: The council's treasury management budget outturn was £4.862m against a budget of £4.028m, a £0.834m overspend. This was due to lower property fund dividend income (the Hermes Federated property fund wound up) and changes to the MRP schedule for Feethams House. The council had anticipated better returns on its £35.408m investment portfolio but actual returns fell short.
findings.matters: Financing costs trending higher than budgeted indicates pressure on the council's ability to manage debt efficiently and suggests reduced investment flexibility, which constrains future financing options.
findings.figures: £0.834m overspend, original budget £4.028m, outturn £4.862m; investments fell from £35.408m to £25.055m
findings.quote: Financing costs overspent on budget by £0.834m due to a decrease in property fund dividends following the ending of one of the Council's investments and the reprofiling of Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charges and repayments for Feethams House following the 2024/25 budget outturn.
